The 2026 Japan Series (日本シリーズ, Nippon Shirīzu; branded as the SMBC Nippon Series 2026 for sponsorship reasons) was the championship series of Nippon Professional Baseball's (NPB) 2026 season. The 77th edition of the Japan Series, it was  a best-of-seven playoff series played between the Central League (CL) Climax Series champion Yokohama DeNA BayStars and the Pacific League (PL) Climax Series champion Fukuoka SoftBank Hawks. This was the second time these two teams met in the Japan Series in just three years, both with identical records from their previous Japan Series matchup. The Hawks swept the BayStars in 4 games to take home their 13th Japan Series championship.
Neither SoftBank nor DeNA suffered a loss in their roads to the Japan Series this season. For SoftBank, they returned to the Japan Series for the third consecutive year, now as the defending champion, after sweeping Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters in the Climax Series Final Stage. This is their 23rd overall appearance. For DeNA, they swept the Yomiuri Giants in the Climax Series First Stage, and then swept the Hanshin Tigers in the Final Stage, winning six consecutive road games to clinch their fifth Japan Series berth in club history.
Game 2 of the 2026 Series was the last game in Nippon Professional Baseball not to feature the designated hitter, as the Central League will adopt the rule beginning with the 2027 season.


== Background ==

The CL seeding was not set until the very last day, October 3, of the regular season, while the BayStars were locked in 3-seed on September 26. On October 3, the Giants were still in the race of clinching the CL Championship, and the Tigers lost earlier that day to Hiroshima Toyo Carp. However, the Giants later lost their final game against the BayStars, and thus they lost the championship to the Tigers and the seeding are locked, with Tigers the 1-seed, Giants the 2-seed, and the BayStars the 3-seed. For the BayStars, on the day they were locked in 3-seed, they were two games above .500 and 7½ games behind the Tigers. They won two of their remaining four games, finishing their season with a .507 record with 7½ games behind the Tigers and preventing the league winner from gaining the two-game advantage in the final stage of CL Climax Series, a new rule added this year for the Climax Series. In the first stage, the BayStars swept the Giants in a best-of-three series, and advanced to the final stage to face the Tigers. Despite having a one-game disadvantage, the BayStars swept the Tigers, winning the first four games of the stage and claimed their ticket to the 2026 Japan Series.
The Fukuoka SoftBank Hawks clinched their third straight PL championship and 22nd overall on September 17, with 11 games remaining. The Hawks secured their 90th win on October 1, and made it impossible for either of the other PL Climax Series teams to come within ten games of them. This also made the new Climax Series rule come into effect, giving the Hawks two-game advantage while changing the final stage into a best-of-seven (race-to-five) series. The Hawks hosted the Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters, the winner of the first stage, and swept the next three games against the Fighters to advance to the Japan Series.


== Summary ==
SoftBank won the series, 4–0.


== Game summaries ==


=== Game 1 ===

Yutaro Ishida started Game 1 for the BayStars, while Naoyuki Uwasawa started for the Hawks. The BayStars loaded the bases in the first inning, but did not score. Ishida pitched 6+2⁄3 innings with five strikeouts, allowed seven hits, and gave up one run. Uwasawa pitched seven shutout innings with four strikeouts, and allowed six hits, none of which are extra base hits.
In the top of the seventh inning, the Hawks once again reached scoring position, this time with Taisei Makihara's single and Yūdai Yamamoto's double. Makihara scored on Yudai Shoji's RBI groundout. Shugo Maki's solo home run in the eighth inning tied the game, and the game remained tied after the 9th, forcing extra innings. In the bottom of the tenth, the BayStars advanced a runner to third base, but stranded him. In the top of the 11th, with runners at first and second with one out, Shoji hit a double, scoring a go-ahead run. The Hawks scored the third run with sacrifice fly by Tatsuru Yanagimachi. Kazuki Sugiyama closed it out at the bottom of the inning to seal the win for the Hawks.
Maki tied the record for the most putouts in one game as a second baseman, with nine. He is the second player in NPB history ever to do so, the first being Masuho Maeda, in the Game 5 of 1970 Japan Series.


=== Game 2 ===

In the bottom of the second inning with one out, the BayStars had two runners in scoring position with a single by Shion Matsuo and a double by Tomoya Inoue. However, Liván Moinelo struck out Shuto Naruse, then intentionally walked Tatsuo Ebina to face Shuto Ogata. With the bases loaded, Moinelo struck out Ogata in three pitches to get out of the jam.
The Hawks scored first with Tomoya Masaki's solo home run in the top of the third inning. They scored another run in the top of the fourth with Yudai Shoji's RBI double.
Moinelo threw seven shutout innings with eight strikeouts, and allowed 5 hits, two of which were doubles by Inoue. After seven scoreless innings, the BayStars had a scoring chance in the eighth, with Ryuki Watarai's single and Shugo Maki reaching on base with a hit by pitch. Yoshitomo Tsutsugo hit a 3-run home run to flip the table, helping the BayStars take a 3–2 lead. However, not long after, in the next frame, the Hawks tied the game with a solo home run by pinch hitter Hotaka Yamakawa. With runners in scoring position and a chance for a walk-off, the BayStars stranded them in the bottom of the ninth, sending the game into extra innings.
In the top of the tenth inning, Yuto Kawamura hit a home run to give the Hawks the lead. This was his first home run since 2024, and only the second of his career. Sugiyama closed out the game to secure the second win for the Hawks.


=== Game 3 ===

The game went scoreless during the first four innings. During these innings, both teams had five ground balls that resulted in a double play, four of which were by the Hawks.
In the top of the fifth inning, Toshiro Miyazaki hit a single to center field, then Masaki Mimori hit a ground ball to the short stop that resulted in a force out at second. After Haru Matsumoto struck out Tomoya Inoue, Mimori stole second base during Takeru Furuichi's at-bat, and later scored on Furuichi's single to the center, giving the BayStars 1–0 lead. Furuichi attempted to reach for second base during the throw, but failed and was out at second base, ending the frame. The BayStars had another chance with runners at second and third during the next inning, but both runners got stranded.
Katsuki Azuma started Game 3 for the BayStars, while Haru Matsumoto started for the Hawks. Azuma threw seven shutout innings, with three strikeouts, two walks and two hit by pitches, and allowed 6 singles. Matsumoto, on the other hand, threw six innings with five strikeouts, allowed six hits, and gave up one run.
The game proceeded to the last inning without any team scoring. In the bottom of the ninth, Ryoya Kurihara reached scoring position with a double, however closer Sean Reynolds retired Yuki Yanagita on a fly ball to left field and struck out Hotaka Yamakawa, preventing Kurihara from advancing on either at bat. With two outs, Itua Ikhine pinch-ran for Kurihara, and scored the game-tying run with Taisei Makihara's RBI single, while Makihara reached second base during the throw. Yūdai Yamamoto was retired immediately after, ending the frame and sending the game to the extra innings for the third time in the series, the first time each of the first three games in the Japan Series went to extra innings in the competition's history.
The game ended with a walk-off home run by Tomoya Masaki in the bottom of the tenth, putting the Hawks up 3–0 in the series, one win away from back-to-back Japan Series championships.
The BayStars defense set a new record in Japan Series history, turning 5 double plays in Game 3, including four grounded-into-double-plays, and a line drive to pitcher that resulted in a double play in the bottom of the seventh. In addition, both teams defense turned 6 double plays in total, also a new record.


=== Game 4 ===

The BayStars took an early lead with a two-run home run by Keita Sano in the first inning, but failed to score for the rest of the game. In the bottom of the fourth inning, Tomoya Masaki walked, then Ukyo Shuto failed a sacrifice bunt, resulting in a force out at 2nd. Shuto stole second base during Kensuke Kondoh's at-bat. After Kentarō Taira struck out Kondoh, the BayStars decided to intentionally walk Ryoya Kurihara to face Yūdai Yamamoto. This plan backfired, as Yamamoto hit a sharp line drive to right field, resulting in a 2-run triple, scoring Shuto and Kurihara. Yamamoto later scored on an RBI single from Yuki Yanagita. The frame ended after the next batter, Hotaka Yamakawa, was retired.
In the sixth inning, Shuto hit a ground ball that deflected off first baseman Sano to right field, and reached second base easily. Shuto then advanced to third on Kondoh's ground ball to second. After Kurihara received a four-pitch walk, Shuto scored on Yamamoto's sacrifice fly to left field. Yanagita retired after, ending the frame.
After the first inning, six Hawks pitchers threw a total of eight shutout innings, with Kazuki Sugiyama closing the game in the top of the ninth for the third time in the series. With Sugiyama striking out Shion Matsuo, the Hawks completed the sweep, and successfully defended their championship. They became the first team in Japan Series history to sweep their Japan Series opponent without having any of their starting pitchers record a win.


== Aftermath ==
With the series win the Hawks' won their back-to-back championship, and their thirteenth overall. The Hawks' finished the postseason this year with a perfect record of 7–0.
Masaki won the Japan Series Most Valuable Player Award and received a six million yen prize. He finished the series with a .348 batting average (7 for 16), and 2 home runs, including the walk-off home run in Game 3.
The Outstanding Player Award went to Kazuki Sugiyama, Yūdai Yamamoto, and Yudai Shoji. Sugiyama made appearances in all four games of the series, and claimed three saves and one win, with a 0.00 ERA. He tied the record for most saves in Japan Series history, and is the first player to claim three saves in Japan Series that ended in a sweep. Yamamoto finished the series with a .364 batting average (4 for 11), with all three runs batted in in Game 4. Shoji finished the series with a .267 batting average (4 for 15), with 3 RBIs and two doubles.
Katsuki Azuma was the Fighting Spirit Award winner. Hawks' captain Yuki Yanagita was once again voted the SMBC Everyone's Cheering Award winner by fans.


== Media coverage ==
The Japan Series was televised in Japan by a variety of television stations and streaming services. Five of the seven games were to be broadcast by TBS, with NHK-BS, Nippon News Network, and TV Asahi also carrying some games.All games were streamed online via TVer, with U-Next, Hulu, and Abema also streaming some games.

The Fukuoka SoftBank Hawks (福岡ソフトバンクホークス, Fukuoka Sofutobanku Hōkusu) are a Japanese professional baseball team based in Fukuoka, Fukuoka Prefecture. They compete in Nippon Professional Baseball (NPB) as a member of the Pacific League. Founded on February 22, 1938, as the Nankai Club, being the first Kansai team to play in Osaka proper, the team went through a few name changes before settling on Nankai Hawks in 1947, eventually changing ownership in 1988 and moving to Fukuoka in 1989. The team subsequently became known as the Fukuoka Daiei Hawks until 2005, when they were purchased by SoftBank Group, becoming the Fukuoka SoftBank Hawks. Since 1993, the Hawks have played at Mizuho PayPay Dome Fukuoka, which has gone under several name changes and seats 40,142 people.
The Hawks are often regarded as one of the most successful franchises in Pacific League and the richest in all of baseball under the ownership of SoftBank Group, with the second most wins in all of Japanese sports, only trailing the Yomiuri Giants. The Hawks have played in the Japan Series 23 different times. The club also won two Japanese Baseball League championships in 1946 and 1948 while the team was based in Osaka. The Hawks' 13 Japan Series championships, including seven championships between 2011 and 2020, and 22 Pacific League pennants, with the most recent of both coming in 2026, are tied for most in the Pacific League with the Saitama Seibu Lions and second-most in all of NPB, only trailing the Yomiuri Giants.
For various reasons, the Hawks experienced a 35 year title drought between 1964 and 1999 including a period of 25 years from 1974 to 1999 without a single Japan Series appearance, despite the relocation to Fukuoka. The drought finally ended in 1999, with gradual additions over the previous five years under new manager and all time home run king Sadaharu Oh. Under Oh (as manager and later executive), Daiei, and later SoftBank, the Hawks embraced internal development and sabremetrics as they eventually formed a baseball dynasty off of a core led by slugger Yuki Yanagita and aces Kodai Senga and Tsuyoshi Wada, capturing Japan Series titles in 2011, 2014, 2015, 2017, 2018, 2019, and 2020, making the Hawks the first team since the 1965–1973 Yomiuri Giants to win more than three consecutive championships.
Through 2026, the franchise's all-time record is 5,885–5,150–412 (.533). The team's current manager is Hiroki Kokubo and the organization's acting CEO is Yoshimitsu Goto.


== History ==


=== Nankai Electric Railway Company ownership (1938–1988) ===
The franchise that eventually became the Fukuoka SoftBank Hawks was founded on February 22, 1938, by Nankai Electric Railway president Jinkichi Terada as Nankai Club (南海軍, Nankai Gun), based in central Osaka. The organization was said to be created as a result of rival railway companies Hanshin Electric Railway and Hankyu convincing Nankai to create a baseball club of their own. While initially met with resistance, the club was admitted to the Japanese Baseball League (JPBL) in the fall of 1938, playing their first games at Sakai Ohama Stadium, but moved into Nakamozu Stadium in the city of Sakai in 1939. The team's name was changed to Kinki Nippon (近畿日本軍, Kinki Nippon Gun) in mid-1944 as wartime austerity measures forced Nankai to temporarily merge with Kinki Nippon Railway. After the 1945 hiatus in the JBL due to the ending stages of World War II in Japan, in 1946 the team's name was changed to Kinki Great Ring (近畿グレートリング, Kinki Gurēto Ringu) and the team won the JBL championship. The name was chosen as a translation of Japan's ancient name, Yamato, in a similar way to the Montreal Canadiens or the New York Yankees.
In mid-1947, when Nankai broke away from Kinki Nippon Railway, they decided to change the team's name, also due to the fact that the name was popular with American soldiers stationed in Osaka, since they also found it funny, and settled upon the moniker they would use until they would sell the team in 1988 – Nankai Hawks (南海ホークス, Nankai Hōkusu). The team was named after Nankai's logo, which, at that time, was a winged wheel. Other names considered were Condors, which was rejected because the Nankai representative who supervised the team was bald, and Cardinals, which was rejected because the club wanted to retain their colors, so they settled on the Hawks moniker.
After the JPBL was reorganized into Nippon Professional Baseball in 1950, the Hawks chose to join the upstart Pacific League alongside the Mainichi Orions, Hankyu Braves, Tokyu Flyers, Daiei Stars, Nishitetsu Clippers, and Kintetsu Pearls. They also moved into the freshly built Osaka Stadium in the ward of Naniwa-ku, Osaka, where they would play until their move to Fukuoka after the 1988 season. Under player-manager Kazuto Tsuruoka (known as Kazuto Yamamoto from 1946 to 1958) they became one of the most successful franchises through the first two decades of the Pacific League's existence, taking two Japan Series championships in 1959 and 1964, as well as 10 Pacific League pennants, an amount that would not be duplicated by the club until 2024. Tsuruoka managed the team from 1946 to 1968, becoming the full-time manager after his retirement as a player in 1952.
In 1964, the Hawks sent second year pitcher Masanori Murakami and two other young players to the San Francisco Giants' single-A affiliate in Fresno as baseball "exchange students". On September 1st of that year, Murakami became the first Japanese player to play in Major League Baseball  when he appeared on the mound for the San Francisco Giants at Shea Stadium against the New York Mets. In his debut, Murakami pitched one inning, allowing one hit and facing four batters in a 1–4 loss for the Giants. Disputes over the rights to his contract eventually led to the 1967 United States – Japanese Player Contract Agreement, which effectively barred Japanese players from playing in MLB until Hideo Nomo exploited a loophole in the contract agreement to join the Los Angeles Dodgers in 1995, although others had tried before, most notably pitcher Yutaka Enatsu, who tried to walk on to the Milwaukee Brewers in 1985, but he was cut at the end of spring training. Murakami returned to the Hawks in 1966, playing for them through 1974. He contributed to the team's 1973 Japan Series appearance, their last under Nankai's ownership.
After player-manager Katsuya Nomura, the last player-manager to win a pennant in NPB, was traded to the Lotte Orions after he, under the influence of his second wife, Sachiyo, tried to float the idea of releasing Hiromitsu Kadota to management in 1978, the Hawks fell straight to the basement for two decades, not finishing with a winning record again until 1999. Following this debacle, Nankai's board of directors and union leadership put pressure on Den Kawakatsu, then-president of Nankai Electric Railways and primary owner of the team, to sell the team, which he refused to do. In response, Nankai's board refused to spend money on the Hawks beyond the bare minimum necessary to keep the team afloat. However, Kawakatsu, who represented the most ardent supporter of Nankai's ownership of the Hawks, died on April 23, 1988, and Nankai immediately put the team up for sale following Kawakatsu's death. The team was sold to supermarket chain Daiei, who moved the team to Fukuoka, to become the Fukuoka Daiei Hawks (福岡ダイエーホークス, Fukuoka Daiei Hōkusu) after the 1988 season.


=== Fukuoka Daiei Hawks (1988–2004) ===
After the franchise was acquired by department store chain Daiei, Inc., the Hawks were moved to Fukuoka for two reasons; the first being the fact that the city had gone a decade without a team in the area, as the Crown Lighter Lions moved to Tokorozawa to become the Seibu Lions in 1978, and the second was that Daiei was looking to expand their reach as a brand to Kyushu, which Daiei had little to no presence in before the acquisition. As a result, they were no longer competing with the Hanshin Tigers, Kintetsu Buffaloes or even the by-then rechristened Orix Braves (later the Orix Blue Wave, now the Orix Buffaloes) for a market share of the Greater Osaka metropolitan area. However, in spite of those efforts of the new ownership, the Hawks still were usually in the cellar of the Pacific League, and continued to be at the bottom half of the league until 1997. The Hawks would play their first four seasons in Fukuoka at the Lions' old home of Heiwadai Stadium.
In 1993, the Hawks moved out of Heiwadai Stadium and into the newly constructed Fukuoka Dome, now known as Mizuho PayPay Dome Fukuoka, located 2.2 kilometers northwest of Heiwadai Stadium's former grounds. Heiwadai Stadium would later be closed in November 1997 and fully demolished by 2008. The Fukuoka Dome would be the first retractable roof stadium in NPB and the only retractable roof stadium until 2023, when Es Con Field Hokkaido opened. However, due to inefficient design, high operating costs, and the rainy climate of Fukuoka, the roof is only opened on special occasions (e.g. on Children's Day and other holidays) when the weather is clear, or if the Hawks win and there is a 30% or less chance of precipitation and the wind speed at 10 meters above the roof is 10 meters per second or slower. Since the Hawks moved to the Fukuoka Dome, they have led Pacific League in annual average attendance every single year except for 2021, where pandemic restrictions in Japan prevented them from reaching said goal.
The Hawks front office adopted a strategy of drafting and developing younger players, supplemented by free agent signings, a policy overseen by team president Ryuzo Setoyama and his aides. Setoyama's most brilliant moves were the hiring of home run king Sadaharu Oh in 1995 to take the reins of manager, a title he would hold until 2008 before he moved into the general manager's position. As of 2026, Oh is still with the Hawks organization as a chairman of the Hawks' board of directors, and still engages with day-to-day operations of the team at the age of 86. Oh replaced then-manager Rikuo Nemoto, who was named team president and held that position until his death in 1999.  Also tapped was Akira Ishikawa, a little-known former player, who was tasked with bringing in talented amateurs. He brought in the likes of Kenji Johjima, Kazumi Saitoh, Nobuhiko Matsunaka, Tadahito Iguchi, Munenori Kawasaki, and future team captain and current manager Hiroki Kokubo through the draft, all of whom went on to become stars for the Hawks.
Supplementing the amateur signings were some notable free-agent acquisitions. Daiei competed with the then richest man in Japan, Yoshiaki Tsutsumi, to pull former Seibu stars from their 1980s championship teams to Fukuoka. Among them were infielder Hiromichi Ishige, outfielder and Hawks manager from 2008 to 2014 Koji Akiyama, and left-handed pitcher and former manager Kimiyasu Kudoh.
These moves, alongside a few unpopular cost-cutting measures, helped to make the Hawks gradually more competitive with each passing year, and in 1999, the team finally broke through. That season, Daiei made their first Japan Series appearance since 1973 (and first as a Fukuoka team), and defeated the Chunichi Dragons in five games, giving them their first championship since 1964. Kudoh was dominant in his Game 1 start (complete game, 13 strikeouts), and Akiyama was named the 1999 Japan Series's most valuable player.
The following year, the Hawks again made the Japan Series, but this time lost to the Yomiuri Giants in six games, which saw two of the greatest players in NPB history, Oh and fellow Giants legend Shigeo Nagashima, face off as managers of their respective clubs. Despite the shaky financial ground that Daiei was on thanks to their rampant expansion in bubble-era Japan, the team continued to be competitive.     ", "url": "https://npb.jp/"}, {"fetched_at": "2026-11-05T11:18:30.805704Z", "note": "wikipedia extract title='2026 Japan Series'", "role": "report", "sha256": "46a04b730ffbdba56032c97c1c37718bc749607fa47fb3513cb72881781c8696", "text": "The 2026 Japan Series (日本シリーズ, Nippon Shirīzu; branded as the SMBC Nippon Series 2026 for sponsorship reasons) was the championship series of Nippon Professional Baseball's (NPB) 2026 season. The 77th edition of the Japan Series, it was a best-of-seven playoff series played between the Central League (CL) Climax Series champion Yokohama DeNA BayStars and the Pacific League (PL) Climax Series champion Fukuoka SoftBank Hawks. This was the second time these two teams met in the Japan Series in just three years, both with identical records from their previous Japan Series matchup. The Hawks swept the BayStars in 4 games to take home their 13th Japan Series championship. Neither SoftBank nor DeNA suffered a loss in their roads to the Japan Series this season. For SoftBank, they returned to the Japan Series for the third consecutive year, now as the defending champion, after sweeping Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters in the Climax Series Final Stage. This is their 23rd overall appearance. For DeNA, they swept the Yomiuri Giants in the Climax Series First Stage, and then swept the Hanshin Tigers in the Final Stage, winning six consecutive road games to clinch their fifth Japan Series berth in club history. Game 2 of the 2026 Series was the last game in Nippon Professional Baseball not to feature the designated hitter, as the Central League will adopt the rule beginning with the 2027 season. == Background == The CL seeding was not set until the very last day, October 3, of the regular season, while the BayStars were locked in 3-seed on September 26. On October 3, the Giants were still in the race of clinching the CL Championship, and the Tigers lost earlier that day to Hiroshima Toyo Carp. However, the Giants later lost their final game against the BayStars, and thus they lost the championship to the Tigers and the seeding are locked, with Tigers the 1-seed, Giants the 2-seed, and the BayStars the 3-seed. For the BayStars, on the day they were locked in 3-seed, they were two games above .500 and 7½ games behind the Tigers. They won two of their remaining four games, finishing their season with a .507 record with 7½ games behind the Tigers and preventing the league winner from gaining the two-game advantage in the final stage of CL Climax Series, a new rule added this year for the Climax Series. In the first stage, the BayStars swept the Giants in a best-of-three series, and advanced to the final stage to face the Tigers. Despite having a one-game disadvantage, the BayStars swept the Tigers, winning the first four games of the stage and claimed their ticket to the 2026 Japan Series. The Fukuoka SoftBank Hawks clinched their third straight PL championship and 22nd overall on September 17, with 11 games remaining. The Hawks secured their 90th win on October 1, and made it impossible for either of the other PL Climax Series teams to come within ten games of them. This also made the new Climax Series rule come into effect, giving the Hawks two-game advantage while changing the final stage into a best-of-seven (race-to-five) series. The Hawks hosted the Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters, the winner of the first stage, and swept the next three games against the Fighters to advance to the Japan Series. == Summary == SoftBank won the series, 4–0. == Game summaries == === Game 1 === Yutaro Ishida started Game 1 for the BayStars, while Naoyuki Uwasawa started for the Hawks. The BayStars loaded the bases in the first inning, but did not score. Ishida pitched 6+2⁄3 innings with five strikeouts, allowed seven hits, and gave up one run. Uwasawa pitched seven shutout innings with four strikeouts, and allowed six hits, none of which are extra base hits. In the top of the seventh inning, the Hawks once again reached scoring position, this time with Taisei Makihara's single and Yūdai Yamamoto's double. Makihara scored on Yudai Shoji's RBI groundout. Shugo Maki's solo home run in the eighth inning tied the game, and the game remained tied after the 9th, forcing extra innings. In the bottom of the tenth, the BayStars advanced a runner to third base, but stranded him. In the top of the 11th, with runners at first and second with one out, Shoji hit a double, scoring a go-ahead run. The Hawks scored the third run with sacrifice fly by Tatsuru Yanagimachi. Kazuki Sugiyama closed it out at the bottom of the inning to seal the win for the Hawks. Maki tied the record for the most putouts in one game as a second baseman, with nine. He is the second player in NPB history ever to do so, the first being Masuho Maeda, in the Game 5 of 1970 Japan Series. === Game 2 === In the bottom of the second inning with one out, the BayStars had two runners in scoring position with a single by Shion Matsuo and a double by Tomoya Inoue. However, Liván Moinelo struck out Shuto Naruse, then intentionally walked Tatsuo Ebina to face Shuto Ogata. With the bases loaded, Moinelo struck out Ogata in three pitches to get out of the jam. The Hawks scored first with Tomoya Masaki's solo home run in the top of the third inning. They scored another run in the top of the fourth with Yudai Shoji's RBI double. Moinelo threw seven shutout innings with eight strikeouts, and allowed 5 hits, two of which were doubles by Inoue. After seven scoreless innings, the BayStars had a scoring chance in the eighth, with Ryuki Watarai's single and Shugo Maki reaching on base with a hit by pitch. Yoshitomo Tsutsugo hit a 3-run home run to flip the table, helping the BayStars take a 3–2 lead. However, not long after, in the next frame, the Hawks tied the game with a solo home run by pinch hitter Hotaka Yamakawa. With runners in scoring position and a chance for a walk-off, the BayStars stranded them in the bottom of the ninth, sending the game into extra innings. In the top of the tenth inning, Yuto Kawamura hit a home run to give the Hawks the lead. This was his first home run since 2024, and only the second of his career. Sugiyama closed out the game to secure the second win for the Hawks. === Game 3 === The game went scoreless during the first four innings. During these innings, both teams had five ground balls that resulted in a double play, four of which were by the Hawks. In the top of the fifth inning, Toshiro Miyazaki hit a single to center field, then Masaki Mimori hit a ground ball to the short stop that resulted in a force out at second. After Haru Matsumoto struck out Tomoya Inoue, Mimori stole second base during Takeru Furuichi's at-bat, and later scored on Furuichi's single to the center, giving the BayStars 1–0 lead. Furuichi attempted to reach for second base during the throw, but failed and was out at second base, ending the frame. The BayStars had another chance with runners at second and third during the next inning, but both runners got stranded. Katsuki Azuma started Game 3 for the BayStars, while Haru Matsumoto started for the Hawks. Azuma threw seven shutout innings, with three strikeouts, two walks and two hit by pitches, and allowed 6 singles. Matsumoto, on the other hand, threw six innings with five strikeouts, allowed six hits, and gave up one run. The game proceeded to the last inning without any team scoring. In the bottom of the ninth, Ryoya Kurihara reached scoring position with a double, however closer Sean Reynolds retired Yuki Yanagita on a fly ball to left field and struck out Hotaka Yamakawa, preventing Kurihara from advancing on either at bat. With two outs, Itua Ikhine pinch-ran for Kurihara, and scored the game-tying run with Taisei Makihara's RBI single, while Makihara reached second base during the throw. Yūdai Yamamoto was retired immediately after, ending the frame and sending the game to the extra innings for the third time in the series, the first time each of the first three games in the Japan Series went to extra innings in the competition's history. The game ended with a walk-off home run by Tomoya Masaki in the bottom of the tenth, putting the Hawks up 3–0 in the series, one win away from back-to-back Japan Series championships. The BayStars defense set a new record in Japan Series history, turning 5 double plays in Game 3, including four grounded-into-double-plays, and a line drive to pitcher that resulted in a double play in the bottom of the seventh. In addition, both teams defense turned 6 double plays in total, also a new record. === Game 4 === The BayStars took an early lead with a two-run home run by Keita Sano in the first inning, but failed to score for the rest of the game. In the bottom of the fourth inning, Tomoya Masaki walked, then Ukyo Shuto failed a sacrifice bunt, resulting in a force out at 2nd. Shuto stole second base during Kensuke Kondoh's at-bat. After Kentarō Taira struck out Kondoh, the BayStars decided to intentionally walk Ryoya Kurihara to face Yūdai Yamamoto. This plan backfired, as Yamamoto hit a sharp line drive to right field, resulting in a 2-run triple, scoring Shuto and Kurihara. Yamamoto later scored on an RBI single from Yuki Yanagita. The frame ended after the next batter, Hotaka Yamakawa, was retired. In the sixth inning, Shuto hit a ground ball that deflected off first baseman Sano to right field, and reached second base easily. Shuto then advanced to third on Kondoh's ground ball to second. After Kurihara received a four-pitch walk, Shuto scored on Yamamoto's sacrifice fly to left field. Yanagita retired after, ending the frame. After the first inning, six Hawks pitchers threw a total of eight shutout innings, with Kazuki Sugiyama closing the game in the top of the ninth for the third time in the series. With Sugiyama striking out Shion Matsuo, the Hawks completed the sweep, and successfully defended their championship. They became the first team in Japan Series history to sweep their Japan Series opponent without having any of their starting pitchers record a win. == Aftermath == With the series win the Hawks' won their back-to-back championship, and their thirteenth overall. The Hawks' finished the postseason this year with a perfect record of 7–0. Masaki won the Japan Series Most Valuable Player Award and received a six million yen prize. He finished the series with a .348 batting average (7 for 16), and 2 home runs, including the walk-off home run in Game 3. The Outstanding Player Award went to Kazuki Sugiyama, Yūdai Yamamoto, and Yudai Shoji. Sugiyama made appearances in all four games of the series, and claimed three saves and one win, with a 0.00 ERA. He tied the record for most saves in Japan Series history, and is the first player to claim three saves in Japan Series that ended in a sweep. Yamamoto finished the series with a .364 batting average (4 for 11), with all three runs batted in in Game 4. Shoji finished the series with a .267 batting average (4 for 15), with 3 RBIs and two doubles. Katsuki Azuma was the Fighting Spirit Award winner. Hawks' captain Yuki Yanagita was once again voted the SMBC Everyone's Cheering Award winner by fans. == Media coverage == The Japan Series was televised in Japan by a variety of television stations and streaming services. Five of the seven games were to be broadcast by TBS, with NHK-BS, Nippon News Network, and TV Asahi also carrying some games.All games were streamed online via TVer, with U-Next, Hulu, and Abema also streaming some games. == See also == 2026 World Series 2026 Korean Series == References ==", "url": "https://en.wikipedia.org/w/api.php?action=query&prop=extracts&explaintext=1&titles=2026+Japan+Series&format=json&redirects=1"}, {"fetched_at": "2026-11-05T11:18:31.021741Z", "note": "wikipedia extract title='Fukuoka SoftBank Hawks'", "role": "report", "sha256": "8b10b3471082e6c41ca30b318539e96384da5614099450af67526763b5a915f8", "text": "The Fukuoka SoftBank Hawks (福岡ソフトバンクホークス, Fukuoka Sofutobanku Hōkusu) are a Japanese professional baseball team based in Fukuoka, Fukuoka Prefecture. They compete in Nippon Professional Baseball (NPB) as a member of the Pacific League. Founded on February 22, 1938, as the Nankai Club, being the first Kansai team to play in Osaka proper, the team went through a few name changes before settling on Nankai Hawks in 1947, eventually changing ownership in 1988 and moving to Fukuoka in 1989. The team subsequently became known as the Fukuoka Daiei Hawks until 2005, when they were purchased by SoftBank Group, becoming the Fukuoka SoftBank Hawks. Since 1993, the Hawks have played at Mizuho PayPay Dome Fukuoka, which has gone under several name changes and seats 40,142 people. The Hawks are often regarded as one of the most successful franchises in Pacific League and the richest in all of baseball under the ownership of SoftBank Group, with the second most wins in all of Japanese sports, only trailing the Yomiuri Giants. The Hawks have played in the Japan Series 23 different times. The club also won two Japanese Baseball League championships in 1946 and 1948 while the team was based in Osaka. The Hawks' 13 Japan Series championships, including seven championships between 2011 and 2020, and 22 Pacific League pennants, with the most recent of both coming in 2026, are tied for most in the Pacific League with the Saitama Seibu Lions and second-most in all of NPB, only trailing the Yomiuri Giants. For various reasons, the Hawks experienced a 35 year title drought between 1964 and 1999 including a period of 25 years from 1974 to 1999 without a single Japan Series appearance, despite the relocation to Fukuoka. The drought finally ended in 1999, with gradual additions over the previous five years under new manager and all time home run king Sadaharu Oh. Under Oh (as manager and later executive), Daiei, and later SoftBank, the Hawks embraced internal development and sabremetrics as they eventually formed a baseball dynasty off of a core led by slugger Yuki Yanagita and aces Kodai Senga and Tsuyoshi Wada, capturing Japan Series titles in 2011, 2014, 2015, 2017, 2018, 2019, and 2020, making the Hawks the first team since the 1965–1973 Yomiuri Giants to win more than three consecutive championships. Through 2026, the franchise's all-time record is 5,885–5,150–412 (.533). The team's current manager is Hiroki Kokubo and the organization's acting CEO is Yoshimitsu Goto. == History == === Nankai Electric Railway Company ownership (1938–1988) === The franchise that eventually became the Fukuoka SoftBank Hawks was founded on February 22, 1938, by Nankai Electric Railway president Jinkichi Terada as Nankai Club (南海軍, Nankai Gun), based in central Osaka. The organization was said to be created as a result of rival railway companies Hanshin Electric Railway and Hankyu convincing Nankai to create a baseball club of their own. While initially met with resistance, the club was admitted to the Japanese Baseball League (JPBL) in the fall of 1938, playing their first games at Sakai Ohama Stadium, but moved into Nakamozu Stadium in the city of Sakai in 1939. The team's name was changed to Kinki Nippon (近畿日本軍, Kinki Nippon Gun) in mid-1944 as wartime austerity measures forced Nankai to temporarily merge with Kinki Nippon Railway. After the 1945 hiatus in the JBL due to the ending stages of World War II in Japan, in 1946 the team's name was changed to Kinki Great Ring (近畿グレートリング, Kinki Gurēto Ringu) and the team won the JBL championship. The name was chosen as a translation of Japan's ancient name, Yamato, in a similar way to the Montreal Canadiens or the New York Yankees. In mid-1947, when Nankai broke away from Kinki Nippon Railway, they decided to change the team's name, also due to the fact that the name was popular with American soldiers stationed in Osaka, since they also found it funny, and settled upon the moniker they would use until they would sell the team in 1988 – Nankai Hawks (南海ホークス, Nankai Hōkusu). The team was named after Nankai's logo, which, at that time, was a winged wheel. Other names considered were Condors, which was rejected because the Nankai representative who supervised the team was bald, and Cardinals, which was rejected because the club wanted to retain their colors, so they settled on the Hawks moniker. After the JPBL was reorganized into Nippon Professional Baseball in 1950, the Hawks chose to join the upstart Pacific League alongside the Mainichi Orions, Hankyu Braves, Tokyu Flyers, Daiei Stars, Nishitetsu Clippers, and Kintetsu Pearls. They also moved into the freshly built Osaka Stadium in the ward of Naniwa-ku, Osaka, where they would play until their move to Fukuoka after the 1988 season. Under player-manager Kazuto Tsuruoka (known as Kazuto Yamamoto from 1946 to 1958) they became one of the most successful franchises through the first two decades of the Pacific League's existence, taking two Japan Series championships in 1959 and 1964, as well as 10 Pacific League pennants, an amount that would not be duplicated by the club until 2024. Tsuruoka managed the team from 1946 to 1968, becoming the full-time manager after his retirement as a player in 1952. In 1964, the Hawks sent second year pitcher Masanori Murakami and two other young players to the San Francisco Giants' single-A affiliate in Fresno as baseball "exchange students". On September 1st of that year, Murakami became the first Japanese player to play in Major League Baseball when he appeared on the mound for the San Francisco Giants at Shea Stadium against the New York Mets. In his debut, Murakami pitched one inning, allowing one hit and facing four batters in a 1–4 loss for the Giants. Disputes over the rights to his contract eventually led to the 1967 United States – Japanese Player Contract Agreement, which effectively barred Japanese players from playing in MLB until Hideo Nomo exploited a loophole in the contract agreement to join the Los Angeles Dodgers in 1995, although others had tried before, most notably pitcher Yutaka Enatsu, who tried to walk on to the Milwaukee Brewers in 1985, but he was cut at the end of spring training. Murakami returned to the Hawks in 1966, playing for them through 1974. He contributed to the team's 1973 Japan Series appearance, their last under Nankai's ownership. After player-manager Katsuya Nomura, the last player-manager to win a pennant in NPB, was traded to the Lotte Orions after he, under the influence of his second wife, Sachiyo, tried to float the idea of releasing Hiromitsu Kadota to management in 1978, the Hawks fell straight to the basement for two decades, not finishing with a winning record again until 1999. Following this debacle, Nankai's board of directors and union leadership put pressure on Den Kawakatsu, then-president of Nankai Electric Railways and primary owner of the team, to sell the team, which he refused to do. In response, Nankai's board refused to spend money on the Hawks beyond the bare minimum necessary to keep the team afloat. However, Kawakatsu, who represented the most ardent supporter of Nankai's ownership of the Hawks, died on April 23, 1988, and Nankai immediately put the team up for sale following Kawakatsu's death. The team was sold to supermarket chain Daiei, who moved the team to Fukuoka, to become the Fukuoka Daiei Hawks (福岡ダイエーホークス, Fukuoka Daiei Hōkusu) after the 1988 season. === Fukuoka Daiei Hawks (1988–2004) === After the franchise was acquired by department store chain Daiei, Inc., the Hawks were moved to Fukuoka for two reasons; the first being the fact that the city had gone a decade without a team in the area, as the Crown Lighter Lions moved to Tokorozawa to become the Seibu Lions in 1978, and the second was that Daiei was looking to expand their reach as a brand to Kyushu, which Daiei had little to no presence in before the acquisition. As a result, they were no longer competing with the Hanshin Tigers, Kintetsu Buffaloes or even the by-then rechristened Orix Braves (later the Orix Blue Wave, now the Orix Buffaloes) for a market share of the Greater Osaka metropolitan area. However, in spite of those efforts of the new ownership, the Hawks still were usually in the cellar of the Pacific League, and continued to be at the bottom half of the league until 1997. The Hawks would play their first four seasons in Fukuoka at the Lions' old home of Heiwadai Stadium. In 1993, the Hawks moved out of Heiwadai Stadium and into the newly constructed Fukuoka Dome, now known as Mizuho PayPay Dome Fukuoka, located 2.2 kilometers northwest of Heiwadai Stadium's former grounds. Heiwadai Stadium would later be closed in November 1997 and fully demolished by 2008. The Fukuoka Dome would be the first retractable roof stadium in NPB and the only retractable roof stadium until 2023, when Es Con Field Hokkaido opened. However, due to inefficient design, high operating costs, and the rainy climate of Fukuoka, the roof is only opened on special occasions (e.g. on Children's Day and other holidays) when the weather is clear, or if the Hawks win and there is a 30% or less chance of precipitation and the wind speed at 10 meters above the roof is 10 meters per second or slower. Since the Hawks moved to the Fukuoka Dome, they have led Pacific League in annual average attendance every single year except for 2021, where pandemic restrictions in Japan prevented them from reaching said goal. The Hawks front office adopted a strategy of drafting and developing younger players, supplemented by free agent signings, a policy overseen by team president Ryuzo Setoyama and his aides. Setoyama's most brilliant moves were the hiring of home run king Sadaharu Oh in 1995 to take the reins of manager, a title he would hold until 2008 before he moved into the general manager's position. As of 2026, Oh is still with the Hawks organization as a chairman of the Hawks' board of directors, and still engages with day-to-day operations of the team at the age of 86. Oh replaced then-manager Rikuo Nemoto, who was named team president and held that position until his death in 1999. Also tapped was Akira Ishikawa, a little-known former player, who was tasked with bringing in talented amateurs. He brought in the likes of Kenji Johjima, Kazumi Saitoh, Nobuhiko Matsunaka, Tadahito Iguchi, Munenori Kawasaki, and future team captain and current manager Hiroki Kokubo through the draft, all of whom went on to become stars for the Hawks. Supplementing the amateur signings were some notable free-agent acquisitions. Daiei competed with the then richest man in Japan, Yoshiaki Tsutsumi, to pull former Seibu stars from their 1980s championship teams to Fukuoka. Among them were infielder Hiromichi Ishige, outfielder and Hawks manager from 2008 to 2014 Koji Akiyama, and left-handed pitcher and former manager Kimiyasu Kudoh. These moves, alongside a few unpopular cost-cutting measures, helped to make the Hawks gradually more competitive with each passing year, and in 1999, the team finally broke through. That season, Daiei made their first Japan Series appearance since 1973 (and first as a Fukuoka team), and defeated the Chunichi Dragons in five games, giving them their first championship since 1964. Kudoh was dominant in his Game 1 start (complete game, 13 strikeouts), and Akiyama was named the 1999 Japan Series's most valuable player. The following year, the Hawks again made the Japan Series, but this time lost to the Yomiuri Giants in six games, which saw two of the greatest players in NPB history, Oh and fellow Giants legend Shigeo Nagashima, face off as managers of their respective clubs. Despite the shaky financial ground that Daiei was on thanks to their rampant expansion in bubble-era Japan, the team continued to be competitive.
